candidates.name: pdf-acroform-court-form-filler
candidates.description: Fill an interactive (AcroForm) PDF such as California SC-100 from a prose case description. Enumerate fields and tooltips to map semantics, discover each checkbox's real on-state from appearance states instead of guessing, fill case-derived text values, and answer EVERY required paired Yes/No eligibility question (negative option when the narrative is silent on the condition; derive count/amount-based answers from the stated facts) while leaving page-1 court caption fields and unmentioned optional subsections empty and standalone opt-in boxes off. Verify by re-deriving the expected answer set from the request and form, then diffing against a fresh value dump and rendered pages, zooming into ambiguous checkbox areas.
candidates.activation: User provides a blank fillable PDF form (court/agency form like SC-100) plus a prose description of the facts, and asks to save a filled copy, filling only necessary fields and using a mandated date format (e.g., xxxx-xx-xx).
avoid: Never guess a checkbox export value (e.g., '/Yes'); read the widget's on-state from /AP/N keys (pypdf) or widget.button_states() (pymupdf) and map [0]/[1] to the printed Yes/No or option-letter labels by position.

Never leave a required paired Yes/No eligibility question blank because the narrative is silent: for attorney-fee-dispute, public-entity, filing-frequency and claim-size questions, an unmentioned condition means the required answer is 'No' (or is derived from the stated amount/history), and exactly one option must be on.

Leave every page-1 court caption field empty — court name/address (CourtInfo), case number, case name, trial date/time/department rows, clerk signature/date; do not infer the county court from a party's city.

Keep standalone opt-in checkboxes (attachments, arbitration, claims filed against public entities, military-duty) and optional text subsections (second plaintiff/defendant, alternate mailing address) empty unless the description affirmatively applies them.
Do not sign the signature line; type/print the name and date only.
Do not set only /V for checkboxes — also set /AS (pypdf) or call widget.update() (pymupdf), otherwise the check may exist in data but not render.

Do not declare success after writing; tool execution success is not task success — verify by re-deriving the expected answer set from the request and form, then diffing against a fresh value dump and rendered pages.

procedure.action: Enumerate all form fields with `pypdf.PdfReader(...).get_fields()`: capture full hierarchical names (e.g. SC-100[0].Page2[0]...), field types (/Tx vs /Btn), and the /TU tooltip text, which states each field's meaning (e.g., which checkbox is 'more than 12 claims' vs 'not', 'claim over $2,500' vs not).

Map fields to the printed layout (render pages, dump page text, list widget rects via `page.widgets()`) and classify EVERY question on the form into: required paired Yes/No, required single-choice lettered options (venue), standalone opt-in box, optional text subsection, or court/clerk-filled. Record the classification — it, not the narrative's silence, decides what may be left blank.

For every checkbox to be set, discover its on-state: list /AP/N keys via pypdf (e.g. Checkbox50[0] -> ['/1']) or `widget.button_states()['normal'][0]` via pymupdf, and confirm [0]/[1] semantics by comparing widget rect coordinates with nearby label word positions (`page.get_text("words")`).

Fill only what the step-2 classification allows: (a) case-derived text — party names/phones/addresses/emails, claim amount and reason narrative, incident start/through dates in the mandated xxxx-xx-xx format, venue zip, declaration date + typed name; (b) required selections — venue letter matching the stated reason, payment-demand Yes, filing-frequency and claim-size answers derived from the stated history/amount, AND the negative option of every other required paired Yes/No question (e.g., attorney-client fee dispute -> No, suing a public entity -> No), because silence on the condition IS the answer, not a reason to skip; (c) nothing else — page-1 court caption, optional subsections and opt-in boxes stay untouched. Write via pypdf (/V on text widgets, /V and /AS on checkboxes, `writer.set_need_appearances_writer(True)`) or pymupdf (`w.field_value = ...; w.update()`); track matched targets and assert none are missing before saving. (Counterexample: an externally graded run that omitted the attorney-fee and public-entity 'No' checks failed exactly those two completeness assertions.)

Verify the saved PDF independently: first re-derive the expected answer set from the request and the form's question list (which texts, which Yes/No/venue selections including required 'No' answers, which fields must stay empty), then re-open the output, dump all non-empty/non-/Off field values, and diff in BOTH directions — missing required decisions and extra unsupported fills are equally failures. Render filled pages (pymupdf get_pixmap or pdftoppm) and visually inspect entries and check marks, cropping/zooming into ambiguous checkbox regions. (Counterexample: the failed run's own re-read confirmed only its intended writes and so never noticed the two unanswered required questions.)

verification: Expected answer set is re-derived from the request plus the form's question list BEFORE reading the output: required texts, required Yes/No/venue selections (including required 'No' answers), and fields that must stay empty.

Post-write dump diff: exactly one on-state per required paired question (payment demand, venue, attorney-fee dispute, public entity, >12 claims, claim-size) — a missing required 'No' fails just as an extra unsupported fill does.
Page-1 court caption fields (CourtInfo, case number/name, trial rows, clerk signature/date) and unmentioned optional subsections are absent from the dump; standalone opt-in boxes remain /Off.
Rendered pages (get_pixmap/pdftoppm) show legible typed values and visibly correct check marks; ambiguous checkbox regions re-rendered at higher DPI and cropped for confirmation.
candidates.termination: Stop when the output PDF exists at the requested path, the dump-vs-expectation diff is empty in both directions (all case-derived values and all required Yes/No selections present; court, optional and opt-in fields empty), all dates follow the mandated format, and rendered pages visually confirm the entries and check marks.
limitations: Field names are specific to this SC-100 revision; the enumeration/tooltip-driven mapping and the required-vs-optional question classification are the reusable parts.

The negative default applies only to required paired Yes/No eligibility questions, not to standalone opt-in boxes or optional text sections; classify each question from its tooltip and printed labels on any new form.
One external validation run (skill usage confirmed) failed only the two required-negative checkbox assertions this revision targets; the corrected rule is provisional until re-validated.
No session exercised recovery for missing pypdf/pymupdf, XFA-only forms, or fields that accept data but do not render.

candidates.name: calendar-pdf-meeting-scheduler
candidates.description: Schedule meetings from request emails against a graphical calendar PDF. Parse each email's duration/window/timezone, measure calendar event blocks by vector geometry against the 15-minute gridline axis (not plain text), treat blue-filled blocks as overwritable, solve for the earliest start times that still accommodate ALL requests, then write template-exact reply files and a results.json index, and re-read outputs to verify.
candidates.activation: User supplies a JSON file of meeting-request emails plus a calendar PDF rendered as a day timeline (adjacent horizontal lines = fixed minutes), asks to propose meeting times per constraints (colored blocks, blue = flexible), and to save reply_*.txt files plus results.json with exact date/time formats.
avoid: Do not infer appointment times from a plain text dump alone; block start/end must be measured from vector rect positions against the gridline axis.
Do not assume email availability windows are in the calendar's timezone; convert explicitly stated zones (e.g., PST to the calendar's Eastern Time) before scheduling.
Do not treat blue blocks as busy, and do not treat red/gray/yellow blocks as overwritable.
Do not greedily take each request's own earliest slot if that pushes another request out of its window; search for earliest starts such that all requests fit.
Do not emit unpadded times ('9:00 AM') or ordinal dates ('January 8th'); follow the mandated zero-padded formats.
Do not invent a messageID; if the input lacks one, fall back to the email's array index and note it.

procedure.action: Read the requests JSON first and record per email: duration, date, availability window, and any explicit timezone token in the body (flag windows whose zone differs from the calendar's, e.g. a 'PST' window against an 'Eastern Time' calendar).
Probe PDF tooling before parsing (e.g. `python3 -c "import pymupdf"`, `which pdftotext`); both sessions found PyMuPDF available and used it as the parser.
Dump the calendar page text (`page.get_text()`) to capture the date/timezone header line and the ordered hour-axis labels used later as calibration anchors.

Extract geometry: `page.get_text("dict")` for span bboxes (hour labels, event titles) and `page.get_drawings()` for filled rects with RGB `fill` tuples; keep only large event-sized fills as appointment blocks.

Calibrate y->time: gridline spacing corresponds to the stated minutes per line (15), anchor the first line to midnight, and compensate the ~1-unit block inset (top+1/bottom-1). Convert each block rect to start/end times, and classify blue-dominant fills (B channel > R and high) as flexible/overwritable, all other colors as busy. Example: `mins = round((y - y0) / step) * 15`.
Render the page to PNG (`page.get_pixmap(...)`) and view it to cross-check that measured intervals and color classifications match the visual calendar before scheduling.

Solve jointly: convert every window into the calendar timezone, exclude blue intervals from busy, and search 15-minute-aligned start times for the earliest assignment where ALL requests fit without overlapping busy blocks or each other; backtrack or reorder requests when the greedy order fails (a small recursive solver was used and confirmed the hand-derived schedule).

Write one reply_{messageID}.txt per email using the exact template (day-name date `Monday, March 09, 2026`, zero-padded `hh:MM AM/PM - hh:MM AM/PM`, duration in hours) and a results.json listing filename+recipient pairs; then `ls`/`cat` the outputs to confirm they exist and match the required format.

verification: Block table cross-checked two ways: computed y->time conversion agrees with the rendered PNG image of the calendar.

A programmatic solver (or explicit interval check) confirms no proposed meeting overlaps a non-blue busy block or another proposed meeting, and every meeting lies inside its requester's (timezone-converted) window.
Re-read reply files and results.json after writing: filenames, recipients, template text, zero-padded date/time formats all present.
candidates.termination: Stop when every email has a reply file whose slot satisfies its window and duration, all slots are mutually non-conflicting with non-blue calendar blocks, results.json indexes all replies, and the verification reads pass.
limitations: Task outcomes were not externally validated; correctness of the chosen slots is asserted only by the agent's own solver/visual check.
Blue detection relied on an RGB-dominance heuristic tied to this calendar's palette; other calendars may encode flexible blocks differently.
PST->ET conversion assumed a fixed 3-hour offset without DST validation.
Gridline calibration assumed uniform spacing and a ~1-unit block inset, verified visually only for this PDF.
Input emails contained no messageID field; falling back to array indices for reply filenames is an unverified convention.

gaps: calendar-pdf-meeting-scheduler passed its validation unchanged and is preserved by the backend; it is intentionally not re-emitted here.

The required-negative rule is confirmed by a single validation instance for two SC-100 questions; other forms or stricter graders may demand additional required selections not observed in these trajectories.
Grading criteria for free-text narratives (claim reason/calculation wording) remain unobserved; keep them strictly grounded in the description's own facts.
No trajectory shows dependency installation or fallback when pypdf/pymupdf are absent, so tooling recovery steps are still unobserved.
